    def _repo(start=None):
        for candidate_start in (os.environ.get("G7_REPO"), start, os.getcwd(),
                                DEFAULT_REPO):
            if not candidate_start:
                continue
            candidate = os.path.abspath(candidate_start)
            while True:
                for marker in ("course.py", "machine.py"):
                    if os.path.isfile(os.path.join(candidate, COURSE, marker)):
                        return candidate
                parent = os.path.dirname(candidate)
                if parent == candidate:
                    break
                candidate = parent
        raise SystemExit("set G7_REPO=/path/to/forja")

    def _refuses(exc, what, call, names=()):
        """The refusal `call` must raise, or the mistake named.

        Every refusal in this course names the offender, so `names` are checked against
        the message: an exception of the right family raised for the wrong reason is not
        the refusal the contract asked for.
        """
        try:
            got = call()
        except exc as refused:
            message = str(refused)
            for want in names:
                assert want in message, (
                    "%s refused with %r, which does not name %r" % (what, message, want))
            return refused
        except NotImplementedError:
            raise
        except Exception as wrong:                               # noqa: BLE001
            raise AssertionError("%s raised %s instead of %s: %r"
                                 % (what, type(wrong).__name__, exc.__name__, wrong))
        raise AssertionError("%s returned %r instead of refusing" % (what, got))

    def _s10_constants(s):
        """`AUDIT_KEYS`, the eleven reasons in order, the verdicts, a step's keys."""
        assert tuple(s.AUDIT_KEYS) == S10_AUDIT_KEYS, (
            "AUDIT_KEYS is %r; an audit answers %r" % (s.AUDIT_KEYS, S10_AUDIT_KEYS))
        assert tuple(s.AUDIT_REASONS) == S10_AUDIT_REASONS, (
            "AUDIT_REASONS is %r; the reasons are %r in their rule order"
            % (s.AUDIT_REASONS, S10_AUDIT_REASONS))
        assert tuple(s.VERDICTS) == S10_VERDICTS, (
            "VERDICTS is %r; the verdicts are %r" % (s.VERDICTS, S10_VERDICTS))

    def _s10_shape(s, answer, what):
        """The answer's own shape: `AUDIT_KEYS`, rows of `STEP_KEYS`, reasons known."""
        assert isinstance(answer, dict) and tuple(answer) == S10_AUDIT_KEYS, (
            "%s answered %r, and an audit answers %r" % (what, answer, S10_AUDIT_KEYS))
        assert isinstance(answer["steps"], tuple), (
            "%s answered steps %r, and the steps are a tuple of rows"
            % (what, answer["steps"]))
        for row in answer["steps"]:
            assert isinstance(row, dict) and tuple(row) == S10_STEP_KEYS, (
                "%s answered the step row %r, and a step is %r"
                % (what, row, S10_STEP_KEYS))
            assert row["reason"] in S10_AUDIT_REASONS, (
                "%s answered the reason %r, and a reason is one of the eleven"
                % (what, row["reason"]))
            assert isinstance(row["status"], int) and not isinstance(row["status"], bool), (
                "%s answered the status %r, and a status is an int"
                % (what, row["status"]))
        used = []
        for row in answer["steps"]:
            if row["reason"] not in used:
                used.append(row["reason"])
        ordered = [reason for reason in S10_AUDIT_REASONS if reason in used]
        assert tuple(answer["reasons"]) == tuple(ordered), (
            "%s answered reasons %r, and the distinct reasons in rule order are %r"
            % (what, answer["reasons"], tuple(ordered)))
        assert answer["verdict"] in S10_VERDICTS, (
            "%s answered the verdict %r" % (what, answer["verdict"]))

    def _s10_fixtures(s, world, scripts):
        """Every fixture audited by name: `holds`, or `incomplete` for the deadlock.

        The expected record the verdict compares against is the world's own, so a
        verdict of `holds` is a fact about the world and not about this stage.
        """
        verdicts = {}
        for name in scripts.names():
            answer = s.audit(world.machine(7), name, {})
            _s10_shape(s, answer, "the audit of %r" % (name,))
            assert answer["session"] == name, (
                "the audit of %r answered session %r" % (name, answer["session"]))
            expected_verdict = "incomplete" if name == "deadlock" else "holds"
            assert answer["verdict"] == expected_verdict, (
                "the audit of %r answered %r, and the world's own expected record "
                "earns %r" % (name, answer["verdict"], expected_verdict))
            assert answer["steps"], (
                "the audit of %r answered no steps" % (name,))
            for position, row in enumerate(answer["steps"]):
                assert row["index"] == position, (
                    "the audit of %r numbered its rows %r" % (name, answer["steps"]))
            if name == "deadlock":
                assert answer["steps"][-1]["reason"] == "deadlock-reported", (
                    "the audit of the deadlock fixture charged its last row %r, and "
                    "a session the scheduler could not finish is reported as the "
                    "deadlock it is" % (answer["steps"][-1]["reason"],))
            verdicts[name] = answer
        # The same audits on a machine the check has already used: the record's
        # counters are the machine's own deltas from a nonzero mark, so an audit
        # that read the ledger absolutely answers a record no honest expected
        # record matches. The expected record comes from a twin — a second machine
        # warmed identically and replayed by the check's own stage_09 — so every
        # byte the two records carry was earned the same way. The warmer spawns,
        # echoes, waits, deadlocks a blocked reader and reaps it, so the transcript,
        # the spawn ledger, the deadlocks and the terminal all start nonzero. A
        # fixture whose own lines name a fresh machine's pids (`kill -STOP 1`)
        # cannot be replayed on a used machine, and the deadlock fixture is
        # replayed fresh alone.
        for name in scripts.names():
            if name == "deadlock":
                continue
            twin = _s10_warmed(world)
            script = scripts.session(name)
            import stage_09
            expected = stage_09.run_session(twin, {"name": name,
                                                   "lines": script["lines"]})
            machine = _s10_warmed(world)
            warm = s.audit(machine, {"name": name, "lines": script["lines"],
                                     "expected": expected}, {})
            _s10_shape(s, warm, "the audit of %r on a used machine" % (name,))
            assert warm["verdict"] == "holds", (
                "the audit of %r on a used machine answered %r, and the counters "
                "are deltas the mark owes" % (name, warm["verdict"]))
            assert warm["session"] == name
        return verdicts

    def _s10_warmed(world):
        """A machine with every counter already moved: the replay measures deltas.

        One echoed child puts entries on the transcript and bytes on the terminal;
        a blocked reader deadlocks the scheduler and is reaped, so the deadlock
        counter moves and no process is left running to spin a later wait.
        """
        machine = world.machine(7)
        warmer = machine.spawn(("echo", "warmed"))
        machine.advance(1)
        machine.wait(warmer)
        read_end, write_end = machine.pipe()
        reader = machine.spawn(("cat",))
        machine.give(reader, 0, read_end)
        machine.wait(reader)
        machine.signal(reader, "TERM")
        machine.advance(1)
        machine.close(0, write_end)
        return machine

    def _s10_evidence(s, world, scripts):
        """The reasons are the evidence's: a wrong expected record changes nothing.

        Each fixture is audited a second time with the world's own expected record
        replaced by one that disagrees on `stdout`, and the answer must keep the
        same steps' reasons — only the verdict moves, to `differs`, and the last
        step row names the key that differed.
        """
        for name in scripts.names():
            script = scripts.session(name)
            wrong = dict(script["expected"], stdout=b"check10: not the world's bytes\n")
            answer = s.audit(world.machine(7),
                             {"name": name, "lines": script["lines"],
                              "expected": wrong}, {})
            _s10_shape(s, answer, "the audit of %r against a wrong expected" % (name,))
            plain = s.audit(world.machine(7), {"name": name, "lines": script["lines"],
                                               "expected": script["expected"]}, {})
            assert answer["reasons"] == plain["reasons"], (
                "the audit of %r answered reasons %r against a wrong expected and %r "
                "against the world's own, and a reason is decided from the evidence"
                % (name, answer["reasons"], plain["reasons"]))
            expected_verdict = "incomplete" if name == "deadlock" else "differs"
            assert answer["verdict"] == expected_verdict, (
                "the audit of %r against a wrong expected answered %r"
                % (name, answer["verdict"]))
            if answer["verdict"] == "differs":
                assert answer["steps"][-1]["command"] in S10_RECORD_KEYS, (
                    "the audit of %r named the difference %r in its last step row, and "
                    "a difference is one of the record's own keys"
                    % (name, answer["steps"][-1]["command"]))
                assert answer["steps"][-1]["command"] == "stdout", (
                    "the audit of %r named %r as the difference, and the wrong record "
                    "disagreed on stdout" % (name, answer["steps"][-1]["command"]))

        The replay is the check's own, on a machine of its own, so the answer key a

        return stage_09.run_session(world.machine(7), {"name": name, "lines": lines})

    def _s10_reasons(s, world):
        """The sessions the world need not hold, and the reason each must reach.

        The expected record each case is compared against is the check's own
        `run_session` replay, so a `holds` verdict says the stage's replay agreed

        was, which is what the case exists to reach.
        """
        wanted = {
            "plain": ("status-from-last-pipeline",),
            "not-found": ("not-found-127",),
            "cannot-execute": ("cannot-execute-126",),
            "redirect": ("redirection-failed",),
            "and-or-left": ("errexit-exempt-and-or-left",),
            "negated": ("errexit-exempt-negated",),
            "background": ("job-not-waited",),
            "signalled": ("signalled-128-plus-n", "job-not-waited"),

        seen = []
        for name, lines in S10_SESSIONS:

            seen.extend(answer["reasons"])
        # `exit 143` is a status a user picked, not a signal's `128 + n`: the audit

        lines = ("exit 143",)
        expected = _s10_expected(world, lines, "exit-picked")

        # A command word that is a variable is matched to the kingdom of the word the

        # A line that cannot be parsed stops the session at the parse status, and the

    def _s10_options(s, world):
        """`errexit` honoured, `condition` believed, an unknown option refused."""
        import rules
        seen = []
        lines = S10_ERREXIT
        expected = _s10_expected(world, ("false",), "options")
        answer = s.audit(world.machine(7), {"name": "options", "lines": lines,
                                            "expected": expected},
                         {"errexit": True})

        assert answer["verdict"] == "holds", (
            "the options case answered %r, and the option's replay is the check's own "
            "expected record" % (answer["verdict"],))
        assert [row["command"] for row in answer["steps"]] == ["false"], (
            "the options case's steps ran %r, and `errexit` stopped the session at "
            "`false`" % ([row["command"] for row in answer["steps"]],))
        assert answer["steps"][0]["status"] == rules.EXIT_FAILURE, (
            "the options case's `false` answered %r" % (answer["steps"][0]["status"],))
        seen.extend(answer["reasons"])

        # A condition's kind is the caller's word: no line records one, so the
        # audit believes `condition` for exactly the lines it names.
        condition_lines = S10_CONDITION
        expected = _s10_expected(world, condition_lines, "condition")
        answer = s.audit(world.machine(7),
                         {"name": "condition", "lines": condition_lines,
                          "expected": expected},

        _s10_shape(s, answer, "the audit of the condition case")

        assert answer["steps"][0]["reason"] == "errexit-exempt-condition", (
            "the condition case's step answered %r" % (answer["steps"][0],))
        seen.extend(answer["reasons"])

        assert plain["steps"][0]["reason"] == "status-from-last-pipeline", (

"""Programs — the ten programs the machine's own process table can become.

Each program is deterministic data: a name, the argv it is normally written
with, a one-line usage, the number of machine steps it costs, and what it does
with its standard input — which the machine itself executes, step by step, so a
pipeline's cost is a number a check can assert and not an approximation.
"""

PROGRAM_NAMES = ("cat", "echo", "env", "false", "grep", "head", "pwd", "sort",
                 "tick", "wc")     # alphabetically sorted, exactly these ten

#: The name, the argv a user usually writes, the usage, the steps it costs, and
#: whether it transforms its input rather than producing from its argv alone.
_PROGRAMS = {
    "cat": {"argv": ("cat",), "usage": "cat",
            "steps": 4, "stream": True},
    "echo": {"argv": ("echo",), "usage": "echo [words]...",
             "steps": 2, "stream": False},
    "env": {"argv": ("env",), "usage": "env",
            "steps": 3, "stream": False},
    "false": {"argv": ("false",), "usage": "false",
              "steps": 1, "stream": False},
    "grep": {"argv": ("grep", "PATTERN"), "usage": "grep PATTERN",
             "steps": 6, "stream": True},
    "head": {"argv": ("head", "-n", "N"), "usage": "head [-n N]",
             "steps": 5, "stream": True},
    "pwd": {"argv": ("pwd",), "usage": "pwd",
            "steps": 2, "stream": False},
    "sort": {"argv": ("sort",), "usage": "sort",
             "steps": 6, "stream": True},
    "tick": {"argv": ("tick", "N"), "usage": "tick [N]",
             "steps": 3, "stream": False},
    "wc": {"argv": ("wc",), "usage": "wc [-l | -c]",
           "steps": 5, "stream": True},
}


def program(name):
    """The record of one program: `{"name", "argv", "usage", "steps", "stdin"}`.

    `steps` is the number of machine steps the program costs, which is the
    number `stage_03.cost_of` sums; `stdin` says whether the program transforms
    what it reads (`True`) or produces from its argv and the machine alone
    (`False`). A name the machine holds no program for is a caller's mistake and
    raises, naming it — because a program that does not exist is a fact about
    the caller's text, and this table is the world's own.
    """
    if not isinstance(name, str) or name not in _PROGRAMS:
        raise ValueError("programs: %r is not a program this machine holds"
                         % (name,))
    spec = _PROGRAMS[name]
    return {"name": name, "argv": spec["argv"], "usage": spec["usage"],
            "steps": spec["steps"], "stdin": spec["stream"]}


def usage_of(name):
    """The one-line usage of `name`, as the machine would print it."""
    if not isinstance(name, str) or name not in _PROGRAMS:
        raise ValueError("programs: %r is not a program this machine holds"
                         % (name,))
    return _PROGRAMS[name]["usage"]

spawned, the signal names it sent, the job table's rows at the end and how
many deadlocks the machine recorded — `SESSION_KEYS`, which is the shape

judgement call.

redirection set applied in order, a background job plus a wait, a trap firing

stopped writer whose reader waits forever — the machine records it, the wait
reports it, and nothing raises).

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 1: The line, the word and the operator.

A line of text, and the two things a shell has to do before anything can run:
split it into the tokens its grammar is written in, and group those tokens into
the lists, pipelines and commands a plan can be made from. Nothing here has a
machine, a program or a descriptor table behind it, which is why every number a
check makes of this stage is a number of bytes and words.

Between the text and the tokens sit the two rules that make a shell's lexer
awkward: a token's bytes are kept exactly as they were written — a quote is not
stripped here, because §4.2 is what decides what a word finally means — and an
operator is matched longest first, because `2>&1` is one operator and not three.
A line a shell cannot read is data, not an exception: `parse` answers the byte
that failed and what it expected there.


DESIGN DECISION — Why are a token's bytes kept exactly as they were written, quotes included?
Because what a word *means* is expansion's business, not the lexer's: `'$X'` and
`"$X"` are the same bytes to a splitter that strips quotes, and two different
answers to the stage that expands them. This stage records what the line wrote —
the quote characters inside `text`, and which form built the word in `quote` —
so every later stage can read the intent off the token instead of guessing it
back from bytes that no longer say. A `quote` field of `mixed` is the honest
answer for `a"b"`: no single form built it, and pretending one did would let a
later stage drop an escape the line wrote deliberately.

DESIGN DECISION — Why are operators matched longest first, and why is `2>&1` one operator?
Because the lexer's greed is the grammar: `>>` read as two `>` tokens is not a
worse answer, it is a different redirection (`>` twice, appending nothing), and
`2>&1` read as `2>`, `&`, `1` is a file named `&1` instead of a copy of fd 1.
Matching longest first is also what makes `2>` an operator only where a token
begins — a digit that opens a word is a byte of that word, so `a2>b` redirects
nothing and names one word — which is the one place a shell's lexer has to know
where it is, not just what it is looking at.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does `parse` answer a failure instead of raising it?
Because a line a shell cannot read is an event, not a crash: a real shell prints
`syntax error` and gives the user the prompt back. So the answer carries the
byte that failed, the rule that broke (`PARSE_ERRORS`), and a sentence naming
what was expected there — and every later stage composes over that shape without
a try/except. The one thing that *does* raise is a line that is not a string at
all, because that is the caller's mistake and not the line's.

DESIGN DECISION — Why is a leading `NAME=value` word kept in `words` as well as in `assignment`?
Because this stage records the line and a later stage decides what the word
becomes: dropping it here would make the splitter the stage that invented the
rule about assignments, and the rule (§4.7: a bare assignment persists, a prefix
does not) is not this stage's to apply. Keeping the word costs nothing and
keeps the record faithful — `X=1` and `X=1 env` are written differently, and the
parse answer says so.
    TOKEN_KEYS      the four fields of one token, in order
    TOKEN_KINDS     the two kinds a token can be
    QUOTE_KINDS     the quoting forms a word can be built from
    PARSE_KEYS      the three fields of a parse answer, in order
    COMMAND_KEYS    the four fields of one command, in order
    PARSE_ERRORS    the five ways a line refuses to read
    tokenize(line)  -> tuple[TOKEN_KEYS], quotes kept as written
    parse(line)     -> PARSE_KEYS, lists or the error that says why not

TODO: implement `tokenize`, `parse` in this file.

TOKEN_KINDS = ('word', 'operator')

QUOTE_KINDS = ('none', 'single', 'double', 'backslash', 'mixed')

PARSE_KEYS = ('line', 'lists', 'error')

COMMAND_KEYS = ('words', 'redirects', 'assignment', 'background')

PARSE_ERRORS = ('unterminated-quote', 'trailing-operator', 'unexpected-operator', 'bad-redirect', 'empty')

_SPACE = ' \t\n'

_COMMENT = '#'

_DIGITS = '0123456789'

    written — quotes and backslashes included, because what a word *means* is
    §4.2's business and this stage only says what was written — and `quote` is the
    one quoting form that built it: `none` for plain bytes, `single`, `double` or
    `backslash`, and `mixed` when more than one form did, which is why `a"b"` and
    `'a'b` are both `mixed` while `'a'` is `single`.

    An operator's `text` is the operator and its `quote` is `none`. Operators are
    matched longest first, so `>>` is one token and `2>&1` is one token and not

    it is the document the redirection carries, so the scanner stops the line at
    the body and marks the delimiter's token, and `parse` answers the body as
    the redirect's target (§4.2: the plan's `<<` file is the body, already
    expanded by the stage that owns expansion)."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _scan()")


def _take_body(line):
    """`(line cut at the body, body or None)`: where a here-document begins.

    A `<<` word followed by a newline and lines that close with the delimiter
    alone is a here-document: the scanner keeps the line up to the delimiter
    word and hands the document back separately. A line with no later lines is
    a `<<` with a file-name word, exactly as a check writes it."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _take_body()")


def _words(line, body):
    """The tokens of the cut line, with the here-document written onto the target."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _words()")


def _lists(tokens):
    """`(lists, error)`: the tokens grouped into the lists, pipelines and commands.

    Every one of `&&`, `||`, `;` and `&` ends the list it follows and begins the
    next, so a list holds one pipeline — unless the line writes `|`, which joins
    commands inside it — and a list is `(pipelines, connector)`: the operator that
    joined this list to the previous one, or `None` for the first. `&` is a
    connector like the others, and the commands of the list it ended keep
    `background` true, so a trailing `&` is visible even though it names no list."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _lists()")


def _command(tokens, at):
    """`(record, next byte, failure)`: the `COMMAND_KEYS` record that starts at `at`.

    A command is the run of words and redirections up to the first operator that
    separates commands, pipelines or lists. A command of redirections only — `> out`
    on its own — is a command: it redirects a shell that runs nothing, which is
    §4.3's business and not this stage's.

    A command that has no word and no redirection is the one way this fails: an
    operator stands where a command has to begin. `|` there is an `empty` pipeline
    — the operator has nothing on its left — and `;`, `&`, `&&` and `||` there are
    an `unexpected-operator`, because a list that never began cannot be ended."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _command()")


def _redirect(tokens, at):
    """`(record, next byte, failure)`: the redirection written at `at`.

    The record is `{"kind", "fd", "target", "quoted"}`: the operator exactly as
    written, the descriptor it redirects, the word it takes as its target — as
    written too, so a quoted file name keeps its quotes — and whether that target
    was quoted, which is the byte §4.2 reads to decide whether a here-document
    expands. `2>&1` takes no word: it makes fd 2 a copy of fd 1, so its target is
    the descriptor the operator itself names.

    A redirection whose word the line never writes is a `trailing-operator`, and one
    whose next byte is an operator instead of a word is a `bad-redirect`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _redirect()")


def _descriptor(operator):
    """The descriptor a redirection redirects.

    `>` and `>>` are fd 1 and `<` and `<<` are fd 0; an operator that carries a
    digit carries its own descriptor, which is why `2>` redirects fd 2 and `2>&1`
    is "fd 2 becomes whatever fd 1 is"."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _descriptor()")


def _leading_assignment(words):
    """The `NAME=value` word a command leads with, or `None`.

    A name is a letter or `_` and then letters, digits and `_`; the value is
    everything the first `=` is followed by, empty included, exactly as written.
    The word stays in `words` as well: this stage records what the line wrote, and
    §4.2 and §4.7 are what decide that a leading assignment is not an argv word."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _leading_assignment()")


def _at_a_command(token):
    """The failure for an operator that stands where a command has to begin."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _at_a_command()")


def _missing(token, what):
    """The failure for an operator whose other side the line never writes.

    The byte that failed is the one the operand was due at — the byte after the
    operator — and not the operator's own first byte: `|` is a token the lexer read
    happily, and what the parser misses is whatever follows it."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 1: implement _missing()")

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 2: Expansion, in the order a shell must.

One text goes in and a tuple of words comes out, and the whole of the stage is
the order the five phases run in: **parameter**, **tilde**, **split**, **glob**,
**quote-removal** (`rules.EXPANSION_ORDER`). Parameter expansion is what puts
whitespace and glob metacharacters into a word that had none, the tilde is what
puts a path where one byte was, and the split and the glob are the two phases that
cut and match what the two before them produced — so a stage that runs them in
another order is not a stage that is slightly worse, it is a stage that answers a
different question. `expand` cuts the whole text and `expand_word` cuts one word;
the split is the one phase whose input is the *provenance* of a byte rather than
the byte, because a space inside a word is the word's own and a space a parameter
put there is a boundary.

The stage never writes the machine and never asks it for a process, a descriptor
or a byte. It knocks on two doors and no others: `machine.files()`, which is the
whole population a pattern is matched against (never a real directory), and
`machine.env()`, which is the only variable source a here-document has, because
§4.2 gives `here_document` no third argument. A failure is an `error` record —
`kind`, `offset`, `detail` — and it answers no payload at all, and a caller's
mistake (a text that is not a string, a state that is neither the shell's own
record nor a mapping of name to string) raises `machine.MachineError` naming the
offender, before a byte of the text is looked at.


DESIGN DECISION — Why do the five phases run in exactly `rules.EXPANSION_ORDER`'s order?
Because the order *is* the answer: a parameter that expands to `a b` must be cut
into two words (parameter before split), a `~` that becomes `$HOME` must cut too
(tilde before split), a quoted space must not cut (split sees provenance), and a
glob metacharacter a parameter produced must match (glob after parameter). Run
the phases in any other order and every one of those answers flips — which is
why the check asks two questions no single phase can answer alone.

DESIGN DECISION — Why is the split the one phase that runs on a byte's provenance rather than the
byte itself?
Because a space is not whitespace everywhere: the space in `'a b'` is content,
the space in `a b` is a boundary, and the two are the same byte. So the phases
carry runs — `literal`, `result`, `quoted`, `escape`, `mark` — and the split cuts
only the boundaries a `result` or an unquoted run made. A flat string would have
thrown the provenance away in phase one.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does `glob` match against `machine.files()` and never against a real
directory?
Because the machine is the world: its filesystem is data, its population is
`files()`, and a pattern's answer has to be reproducible on a machine with no
disk at all. Sorted order is part of the contract — a glob is a set, but a
command line is a sequence — and a pattern that matches nothing answers itself,
because that is what a shell's command line keeps.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does an expansion never apply to its own result?
Because one pass is what a shell does: `$X` where `X='$(echo hi)'` is not
another expansion, it is bytes. Running the scanner again over what a phase
produced would make the answer depend on the *content* of a variable rather
than the line, which is how injection bugs are born. The phases are a pipeline
over the original text, and the result is written back with its quoting
reported — not re-read.
    EXPAND_KEYS     the three fields of an expansion answer, in order
    EXPAND_ERRORS   the four ways an expansion refuses
    expand(m, text, vars)        -> EXPAND_KEYS, the whole text
    expand_word(m, text, vars)   -> EXPAND_KEYS, one word only
    substitute(m, text, vars)    -> {"text", "error"}, phase one alone
    glob(m, pattern)             -> {"paths", "error"}, the machine's own files
    here_document(m, body, q)    -> {"bytes", "error"}, a << body

TODO: implement `expand`, `expand_word`, `substitute`, `glob`, `here_document`
in this file.
"""

import machine

EXPAND_KEYS = ('text', 'words', 'error')

EXPAND_ERRORS = ('bad-substitution', 'unset-variable', 'bad-glob', 'here-document-unterminated')

_LITERAL = 'literal'

_RESULT = 'result'

_QUOTED = 'quoted'

_ESCAPE = 'escape'

_MARK = 'mark'

_SPACE = ' \t\n'

_METACHARS = '*?['

_FIRST = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_'

_REST = _FIRST + "0123456789"


def _refuse(message):
    """A caller's mistake: the offender is named and the machine is not touched."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _refuse()")


def _record(kind, offset, detail):
    """§4.1's error shape: what failed, the byte in the text that failed, and the detail."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _record()")


def _as_text(text, what):
    """The text, or the refusal naming what was handed over instead of one."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _as_text()")


def _state(variables):
    """The variable table and the flags out of the shell's own state.

    The state is the house record — `{"variables": {name: value}, "flags":
    {"nounset": bool}}` — and a bare `{name: value}` mapping is that state with no
    flags on, so the plain call needs no ceremony. The fields another stage owns
    (`exported`, `traps`, `jobs`, `cwd`, `exit`, `args`, `stdin`) are read by
    nobody here and written by nobody here; a mapping that is neither shape, a
    variable whose value is not a string, or an option that is not a bool refuses
    with `machine.MachineError` naming the offender."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _state()")


def _value(table, name, nounset, offset):
    """The value of `name`: itself, nothing, or the `unset-variable` record of the refusal.

    A name that is not set and has no word of its own expands to nothing, and
    under `nounset` to the record that names it — with the offset of the `$` that
    asked for it."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _value()")


def _environment(machine):
    """The machine's own environment as a variable table: a here-document's only source."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _environment()")


def _flat(parts):
    """The bytes of `parts` in order: what a phase has produced, quotes and all."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _flat()")


def _report(parts):
    """The parts written back as the text they came from: quote characters where they stood.

    `_flat` answers the bytes; this answers the text — the marker segments write
    the `'` and the `"` back exactly where the text had them, an escaped byte
    behind its `\`, and a phase's own insertion as the bare bytes it put there —
    so an expansion's `text` is the word with its quoting still as written and
    its parameters already substituted. It is not the caller's input: `"$X"` with
    `X=a b` reports `"a b"`, and a text nothing touched reports itself."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _report()")


def _has_metachar(text):
    """True when `text` holds a byte a pathname pattern would read as a metacharacter."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _has_metachar()")


def _name_is(name):
    """True when `name` is a name a variable may have: a letter or `_`, then letters, digits, `_`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _name_is()")


def _parameter(text, table, flags, base):
    """Phase one: `text` with its parameters expanded, its quotes still as written.

    Answers `(parts, error)`. `parts` is the text cut into runs — `literal` (as
    written and unquoted), `result` (what an expansion or a tilde inserted, also
    unquoted), `quoted` (a run inside `'` or `"`, whose bytes are content like any
    other but never split and never glob), `escape` (the one byte a backslash
    quoted) and `mark` (a quote character itself, which is not content at all and
    is written back only when the text's quoting is reported) — and `error` is
    `None` or §4.1's record, its offset counted from the start of the text this
    phase was handed, `base` being where that text begins in the caller's own. An
    expansion is never applied to its own result: what a `$NAME` is worth is
    bytes, and they are not scanned again."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _parameter()")


def _at_dollar(text, at, table, flags, base):
    """The expansion that starts at `text[at]`: its value, the byte after it, its error.

    A `$` that starts nothing — the last byte of the text, or one followed by a
    byte no name and no `{` can begin with — is a `$` like any other, and stands."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _at_dollar()")


def _braced(text, at, table, flags, base):
    """The `${...}` that starts at `text[at]`: its value, the byte after its `}`, its error.

    The grammar is exactly `${NAME}`, `${NAME:-word}`, `${NAME:+word}`,
    `${NAME#prefix}`, `${NAME%Suffix}` and `${#NAME}`: braces do not nest, the
    word of `:-` and `:+` is expanded once itself, the operand of `#` and `%` is
    literal, and anything else is a `bad-substitution`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _braced()")


def _tilde(parts, table, one_word):
    """Phase two: a leading `~` of a word becomes `HOME`, and nothing else does.

    A tilde is the first byte of a word — the text's own first byte, or the byte
    after an unquoted space — and only when a `/` or the end of the word follows
    it: `~user` is left alone, because this machine has no user table, and a
    quoted or backslashed `~` is a byte like any other. The path arrives as an
    unquoted insertion, so the split that follows cuts it: a `HOME` that carries
    a space makes two words, which is what running this phase before that one
    means. A table with no `HOME` leaves the `~` where it was."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _tilde()")


def _split(parts, one_word):
    """Phase three: the parts cut into fields on unquoted whitespace.

    A run of unquoted whitespace is a boundary and is not itself a field, an
    empty field is not a word — except a field that was quoted, because `""` is a
    word and `$UNSET` is not. `one_word` is the whole of the `expand` /
    `expand_word` difference: a word the lexer handed over is one word, so its
    own literal whitespace stays inside it and only the whitespace a `result`
    segment carries cuts, while a text that may hold several words is cut on
    every unquoted space it has."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _split()")


def _class_end(pattern, at):
    """The byte of the `]` closing the class opened at `pattern[at]`, or `-1`.

    A `]` in the class's first position is a member and not the end — `[]a]` is
    the class of `]` and `a` — and a class the pattern never closes is not a
    class at all."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _class_end()")


def _in_class(pattern, at, close, byte):
    """True when `byte` is a member of the class `pattern[at:close + 1]` names."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _in_class()")


def _match_at(pattern, at, path, which):
    """True when `pattern[at:]` matches `path[which:]`, no part of a pattern crossing a `/`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _match_at()")


def _matches(pattern, path):
    """True when the whole `path` matches `pattern`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _matches()")


def _class_error(pattern):
    """The byte of a `[` whose class is never closed, or `None` when every class closes."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _class_error()")


def _matched(machine, pattern):
    """The paths of `machine.files()` that `pattern` matches, or the `bad-glob` record.

    A pattern with no metacharacter is not a pattern: it answers itself, and the
    machine is not asked at all. A pattern that matches nothing answers itself
    too, because that is the word the command line keeps. Everything else is the
    machine's own population, in sorted order."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _matched()")


def _globbed(machine, fields):
    """Phase four itself: every field that holds an unquoted metacharacter becomes its matches.

    Answers `(words, error)`: `words` is the fields, each globbed one replaced by
    its paths — several words where one was — and `error` is `None` or the
    `bad-glob` record. A metacharacter inside quotes, or one a backslash quoted,
    is a byte like any other and does not make the field a pattern."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _globbed()")


def _word(field):
    """The field's bytes with its quoting resolved: phase five's answer for one field.

    A quote character is not content — it stops splitting and globbing while the
    phases run and it is gone when they are over — and an escaped byte is the
    byte it escaped."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _word()")


def _unquoted(fields):
    """Phase five: the fields with their quotes and their backslashes resolved away."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _unquoted()")


def _delimiter(line):
    """The delimiter a here-document's first line names: its quotes removed, nothing expanded.

    A `$` in the line is a `$`: the delimiter is a word, not a word to be
    expanded, and what its quoting decides is whether the document expands, which
    the caller states with `quoted`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _delimiter()")


def _nothing(error):
    """The record a failed expansion answers: the error, and no payload at all."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _nothing()")


def _expanded(machine, text, variables, one_word):
    """The five phases in `rules.EXPANSION_ORDER`'s order, and the record they answer.

    `text` is the text after the parameter and tilde phases — quotes as written,
    before the split cut it and before the glob replaced it — and `words` is what
    the five left. `one_word` is the whole difference between `expand` and
    `expand_word`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement _expanded()")


def expand(machine, text, variables):
    """The words a whole `text` expands to, by the five phases in their order.

    `text` may hold several words, so the split cuts it on every unquoted space;
    the record is `EXPAND_KEYS` and a failed expansion answers `text = None` with
    no words. `variables` is the shell's state or a bare table, and a record that
    is neither refuses with `machine.MachineError` before a byte is looked at."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement expand()")


def expand_word(machine, text, variables):
    """The words one word expands to: the same phases, cut only where an expansion cut.

    The word the lexer handed over is one word, so a space that was already in it
    stays in it; the whitespace a parameter or a tilde put there splits, because
    that phase ran before this one."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement expand_word()")


def substitute(machine, text, variables):
    """Phase one and nothing else: `text` with its parameters expanded, quotes as written.

    The whole grammar — `${NAME}`, `$NAME`, `${NAME:-word}`, `${NAME:+word}`,
    `${NAME#prefix}`, `${NAME%Suffix}`, `${#NAME}` — and the answer is
    `{"text", "error"}`: the text after the phase, or `None` with the record of a
    `bad-substitution` whose body is outside the grammar, or of an
    `unset-variable` under `nounset`. Nothing here splits, globs, expands a
    tilde or removes a quote."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement substitute()")


def glob(machine, pattern):
    """The machine's own paths that `pattern` matches, in sorted order.

    `machine.files()` is the whole population and a pattern that matches nothing
    comes back as written; a pattern with no metacharacter answers itself without
    asking the machine. Answers `{"paths", "error"}` — `paths` is `None` when
    `error` is the record of a class that is never closed — and a `pattern` that
    is not a string raises `machine.MachineError` naming it."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement glob()")


def here_document(machine, body, quoted):
    """The bytes of a `<<` body: its delimiter's line first, its terminator line last.

    The document is every line between the delimiter line and the first line that
    is exactly the delimiter with its quotes removed, each with its newline, and
    `quoted` says whether that delimiter was quoted: quoted, the bytes stand as
    written; unquoted, parameters expand from the machine's own environment and
    nothing else happens — no split, no glob, because a here-document is bytes
    and not words. Answers `{"bytes", "error"}`, `bytes` being `None` when a
    `here-document-unterminated` or a `bad-substitution` is named instead."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 2: implement here_document()")

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 3: The pipeline, the descriptor table and what a pipe costs.

A pipeline of *N* commands is *N* children and *N - 1* pipes, and every one of those
descriptors is decided before the first child exists: the words of each command are
expanded (§4.2), the pipes are made, and each command's redirections are walked left
to right over the table the pipes left behind. The order is the whole point of the
stage — `echo x >f 2>&1` sends both bytes to the file while `echo x 2>&1 >f` sends
the error wherever fd 1 pointed *before* the redirect — so the plan resolves a
duplication eagerly and the table a stage-4 spawn reads is already the table the
child gets.

Nothing here runs a command, and nothing here writes the machine except through the
calls this stage's own surface is defined to make: `machine.pipe()` once per gap and
`machine.store` once per here-document. Everything else is `machine.exists`,
`machine.is_dir` and the world's own program data, so a redirection that cannot be
made is a record with empty `commands`, `pipes` and `redirects` and a cost of zero
— it has asked for no pipe, no file and no child.


DESIGN DECISION — Why is the whole descriptor table built before anything runs?
Because a redirection that cannot be made must cost nothing: no pipe made, no
here-document stored, no child spawned, and the answer an error with empty
table and zero cost. A plan that built as it went would have already spent
pipes when it discovered the refusal — and then either leaked them or had to
unmake them. Two passes make the promise mechanical: the first validates
purely, the second spends.

DESIGN DECISION — Why do redirections apply left to right, and why is `cmd >f 2>&1` different
from `cmd 2>&1 >f`?
Because each redirection reads the table as it stands: `>f` points fd 1 at the
file, so the `2>&1` that follows copies the file into fd 2 — both go to `f`.
Swapped, `2>&1` copies the terminal into fd 2 *first*, and the `>f` that follows
moves only fd 1. The order is the meaning; a plan that applied them in any
other order would answer a question the user did not write.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does the plan know a pipeline's byte counts and step cost before running?
Because cost is arithmetic over the world's own data — `programs.program(name)
["steps"]` per command, and a writer's output a function of its argv — and a
number the plan can assert is a number a check can hold the run to. It is also
the difference between planning and guessing: `cost_of` asks the program table,
not the machine, so its ledger does not move — planning spends nothing.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does a leading assignment word leave the plan's argv?
Because `X=1 env` runs `env`, not `X=1 env`: the assignment is the shell's
variable table's business (§4.7), and the child's argv is what the child
execs. But the word is not hidden — the parse kept it in `words` — and a
command that is *nothing but* the assignment is `empty-pipeline` here,
because it is not a pipeline command at all.
    PLAN_KEYS      the five fields of a plan, in order
    PLAN_ERRORS    the five ways a pipeline refuses to be planned
    plan(m, pipeline, vars)            -> PLAN_KEYS, the whole table
    redirects_of(m, command, vars)     -> {"fds", "redirects", "error"}
    cost_of(m, names)                  -> int, the machine steps

TODO: implement `plan`, `redirects_of`, `cost_of` in this file.
"""

import programs
import stage_02
from machine import SCALE
from machine import MachineError

PLAN_KEYS = ('commands', 'pipes', 'redirects', 'steps', 'error')

PLAN_ERRORS = ('bad-fd', 'not-a-file', 'ambiguous-redirect', 'unknown-program', 'empty-pipeline')

_STANDARD = (0, 1, 2)

_TERMINAL = 'terminal'

_KINDS = ('>', '>>', '<', '<<', '2>', '2>&1')

_READING = ('<',)

_SILENT = ('false', 'tick')


def _error(kind, target, detail):
    """The plan's refusal: the kind, the offender and a sentence naming what was expected."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _error()")


def _empty(error):
    """What a refused plan answers: no table, no pipe, no record, and no cost."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _empty()")


def _commands_of(pipeline):
    """The pipeline's commands in order, or the refusal naming what is not one."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _commands_of()")


def _words_of(command, index):
    """The words of one command, as written, or the refusal naming the wrong one."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _words_of()")


def _redirects_of(command, index):
    """The redirection records of one command, or the refusal naming the wrong one."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _redirects_of()")


def _expanded(machine, words, variables):
    """Every word's expansion in order: one word may become several, or none at all.

    The expansion is §4.2's, called once per word as written and never again on its
    own result, and a word whose expansion is an error contributes no word — which is
    how a command whose words all expand to nothing reaches `empty-pipeline`."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _expanded()")


def _fd_number(value):
    """A descriptor number, or None when it is not a small non-negative int."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _fd_number()")


def _fd_of(record, kind):
    """The number a redirection names, or the number its kind implies."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _fd_of()")


def _one_word(machine, record, variables):
    """A redirection's target expanded to exactly one word, or the refusal saying why.

    The answer is `(word, None)` or `(None, error)`: a target that expands to no word
    (an unset variable, §4.2) or to several (a split, §4.2) names no one file, and
    that is `ambiguous-redirect` and not a guess."""
    raise NotImplementedError("stage 3: implement _one_word()")


def _applied_table(machine, command, variables, index, ends, store):
    """One command's descriptor table: the standard numbers, the pipes, then the redirections.

    `ends` is `(read_fd, write_fd)` when the command sits in a pipeline and `None`
    when it stands alone; the pipeline is installed *before* the command's own
    redirections are walked left to right, which is the order a shell must use and
    the reason `2>&1` copies the pipe in one case and the terminal in the other.
    `store` is false in the pure pass that validates the plan and true in the pass

child per command, in pipeline order, born with the plan's descriptor table; then the
shell waits for every one of them, because a process that has exited and not been

the first failure — and the machine's own proof that nothing was left behind:

deadlock instead of hanging; the run reports it with `rules.EXIT_FAILURE` rather than
raising, and only the children that actually exited appear in `waited`. A command

the record's own answer. The run reports `EXIT_FAILURE` with the children

exits with 127, and is reaped like any other child. Raising would make the
caller handle a special case that the status already expresses — and 126

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 5: The job table: background, stopped, and who waits for whom.

A process the shell decided not to wait for is still the shell's business: it
has a number the user can name, a state the user can read, and a status nobody
knows yet. The job table is that bookkeeping — one row per pipeline the shell
started without waiting for it, keyed by the small number a job spec names, and
answered from the machine's own process table rather than remembered separately.

about: a `wait` on a job that is already done answers its status without touching
the machine, and a `jobs` listing reaps what has finished but never waits for a
running one. `stop` and `resume` are the shell's mirror of the machine's own
`STOP` and `CONT`, and `resolve` is what turns `%1`, `%+`, `%-` and a pid into
the pid the row holds.

Because a job is a promise about *who waits*: a pipeline started with `&` is
recorded and never waited for, and every other pipeline is waited for before
the shell moves on. Letting any other call create rows would make "who has
been waited for" a property of the caller's discipline rather than of the
table — and the table is the shell's answer to `jobs`, `wait` and `kill` alike.

DESIGN DECISION — Why is the machine's own process table the truth for `running` and `stopped`
while a `done` row is remembered by the shell?
Because the machine knows what it killed, stopped and reaped, and the shell
should not keep a second opinion: `jobs` reads the state off the machine and
reaps what it says has exited. But a `done` job is a fact the machine has
already forgotten — its pid is gone from the table — so the shell remembers
the status, which is the one fact a `wait` on that job still owes the user.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does `jobs` reap finished jobs but never wait for running ones?
Because the two look similar and mean the opposite: reaping is collecting a
status that already exists, waiting is blocking until one does. A `jobs`
listing that blocked would stop the prompt on a long job; a listing that did
not reap would show zombies as running. The line between them is `machine.
reapable()` and it is the whole implementation.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does `resolve` raise on a spec it cannot read instead of answering a row?
Because `%1` is the user's word for a row, and a spec that names nothing is a
caller's mistake at the keyboard — the same kingdom as a pid that does not
exist. The rest of the stage answers data because the shell carries on from a
stopped job or a finished one; there is nothing to carry on from when the
spec names no row at all.

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 6: Signals, traps, and what a signal does to a job.

A signal is the one thing a shell has to carry both ways: it decides what to send, and
it decides what a signal that arrived means. The machine keeps the first half — a
signal is a name, the numbers are `rules.SIGNAL_NUMBERS`, and the default action is the
machine's own: `INT`, `QUIT` and `TERM` kill, `STOP` stops, `CONT` resumes, and a
process that died of a signal answers `128 + n`, which is why `status_of` exists at
all. The shell keeps the second half: a trap is a row in the shell's own table, and
`run_traps` is where the shell's status stops being the command's and becomes the last
trap's.

Nothing about a trap is the machine's. The machine delivers a signal and records what
the process did about it; the shell decides whether a signal it received means "run
this command" (`trap ... CMD`), "do what you would have done anyway" (`""`, the
signal's default) or "never see this again" (`"-"`). `STOP` and `CONT` are not
trappable at all: they are the machine's own words for a job's state, and a shell that
let a trap swallow a `CONT` would have a job nobody could restart.

Because the machine delivers a signal and records what the process did; what
the shell *does about it* — run a command, reset to default, ignore forever —
is the shell's policy, and two shells on one machine may disagree. Keeping
the table in the shell's own state (rows keyed by name, mutated in place) is
what makes `run_traps` composable at any command boundary without the machine
knowing traps exist.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does the status of the last trap to run become the shell's own status?
Because a trap is the shell's own work done at its own boundary: the command
that just finished already had its status recorded, and the trap ran after
it. With two traps due, signal-number order decides which ran last — and the
check pins exactly that, because the other obvious reading (the command's
status survives) is the one a first implementation reaches for.

Because they are not messages, they are states: a `STOP` the shell could
swallow would be a job nobody could see, and a trapped `CONT` a job nobody
could restart. The trappable list is a deliberate subset — `HUP`, `INT`,
`QUIT`, `TERM`, `CHLD` — and a trap on anything else is the caller's
mistake, raised rather than stored.

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 7: The builtins that must not fork.

A shell is a process, and a handful of the words it knows are commands of *that
process*: `cd` changes its working directory, `export` changes its environment,
`shift` moves its positional parameters, `set` changes its own flags, `read` consumes
its input, `exit` ends it, and `:` does nothing whatsoever. Every other word becomes a
child. This stage is that boundary, and it is the only stage whose answer is a status
*and* a change: a state builtin runs in the shell's own process, so the machine is
never asked for a process at all — `machine.stats()["spawn"]` does not move across a
single one of these calls, which is the fact the whole stage is built on.

Every call answers a `BUILTIN_KEYS` row: the word, the status, the *kind* of state
the call wrote, and the bytes it wrote to the shell's stdout. The kind names the
state the call owns — `"cwd"` for `cd`, `"env"` for `export` and `unset`,
`"variables"` for `shift`, `read` and a bare `NAME=value` word, `"options"` for
`set`, `"exit"` for `exit`, `"unchanged"` for `:` and for every call that wrote
nothing at all. The state the call wrote belongs to the caller's record, which this
stage mutates in place: `variables`, `exported`, `flags`, `cwd`, `exit` and `args`
are the shell's own memory, `machine.cwd()` and `machine.env()` are the machine's own
answer key for the two builtins that reach it, and `stdin` is the front of the shell's
own input, which is what `read` consumes and the only way `read` can answer at all.


DESIGN DECISION — Why must a state builtin run in the shell's own process, and why is that
provable?
Because `cd` in a child changes a child's directory and nothing else — which
is why a first implementation so often "works" on the happy path and fails
the session later. The proof is the machine's own ledger: `stats()["spawn"]
does not move across the call. A check that read the source could be fooled;
a check that reads the ledger cannot.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does `run_builtin` mutate the caller's state in place instead of
answering a new state record?
Because the state *is* the shell's process memory: a record answered back
would be a value the caller has to reassign at every call site, and one
forgotten reassignment is a silent fork of the shell's own memory. Mutating
in place makes the builtin's effect visible through every alias the session
holds — the same reason §4.8's condition runs against a copy and a command
runs against the original.

DESIGN DECISION — Why are `trap`, `kill` and `wait` builtins of the shell but refused by this
stage?
Because ownership is the discipline: the tables those three read and write
belong to stage 6 (signals, traps) and stage 5 (jobs), and a stage that ran
them here would need those tables as parameters — which is how two stages end
up with two readings of one table. `is_builtin` still answers true, because
the *shell* owns the words; `run_builtin` refuses, because this stage does not
own the state.

DESIGN DECISION — Why is `exit` masked with `LIMITS["status"]` instead of refused?
Because `exit 256` is a user typing a number the shell accepts and wraps, not
a caller passing a wrong type: the machine's own `exit` refuses outside
0..255, and the shell's job is to translate the user's intent into what the
machine takes. `n & 255` is that translation — the same one a real shell
does — and the check pins both spellings (`exit 256` is 0, `exit -1` is 255).
    BUILTIN_KEYS    the four fields of one builtin answer, in order
    BUILTIN_STATES  the six kinds of state a builtin can write
    is_builtin(name) -> bool
    run_builtin(m, name, argv, state) -> BUILTIN_KEYS

"""Shell From Scratch — stage 8: Lists, conditions and the rules of `set -e`.

A line is more than one pipeline: `&&`, `||`, `;` and `&` decide which of them
runs at all, and `errexit` decides whether a failure ends the line. This stage
runs a parsed line's lists in order — short-circuiting `&&` and `||` on the left
side's status, running `;` unconditionally, and starting a `&` list without
waiting for it — and records every status with the *kind* that says whether
`errexit` may stop on it.

The kinds are the whole of the `set -e` discipline: a condition's status, the
left side of an `&&`/`||`, a negated pipeline and a pipeline's every command but
the last are all exempt, and a plain failure is not. The stage also owns the one
routing rule the contract pins: a simple command whose first word is a builtin
this shell refuses (`trap`, `kill`, `wait`) goes to the stage that owns it, after
expansion, whatever shape the command sits in.


DESIGN DECISION — Why does every recorded status carry a *kind*, and why is the kind decided by
position rather than by the command?
Because `errexit` is a rule about *where* a failure happened, not *what*
failed: `false` in a condition never stops the shell, the same `false` on a
line alone always does. The kinds are the six positions the rule names, and
`exempt(kind)` is the whole of `set -e` — one function, six answers, no
special cases buried in the runner.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does a `!` negation rewrite the pipeline's last row's status instead of
keeping both numbers?
Because `$?` is one number: after `! false`, the shell's status is 0 and the
fact that the pipeline answered 1 is gone from the record. The kind `negated`
is what survives — it tells the audit *why* the status is 0 — and the
pipeline's own answer is deliberately not kept, because a status the shell
does not carry is a status no later rule can read.

DESIGN DECISION — Why is the in-process path taken only for a sole simple command with no `&`?
Because the two promises conflict otherwise: a state builtin must write the
shell's own memory (§4.7), but a builtin *inside a pipeline* is a child's
command by definition, and a background list is the promise that nothing
waits. The rule draws the line exactly where both promises can hold — one
command, foreground, no redirections — and everything else goes to the plan.

DESIGN DECISION — Why does the routing rule for `trap`, `kill` and `wait` live in this stage and
apply to the first word only?
Because a routing decision made anywhere else would be a special case per
composer, and two composers with two readings of `kill -INT %1` after `&&` is
exactly the disagreement the state record was pinned to prevent. First word
because that is what a simple command is: `echo kill` is not a kill. The rule
is blind to shape — inside a list, after `&&`, or the whole line all route
the same way.
    LISTS_KEYS    the five fields of a line's record, in order
    STATUS_KINDS  the six kinds a status can be recorded under
    run_lists(m, lists, state)  -> LISTS_KEYS
    exempt(kind)                -> bool, errexit may not stop on it
    condition_of(m, condition)  -> (status, kind)

"""

one rule that makes the record checkable, that the world already holds the answer.

the user whether to fix a typo or a permission. `128 + n` is not a status at all: it is

        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
